item.title: SME Memory Engine Adds Spatial Regions and Explainable Retrieval
item.description:
SME Memory Engine Adds Spatial Regions and Explainable Retrieval

A new long-term memory engine for AI applications called SME has been released, featuring self-organizing spatial memory regions, Ebbinghaus-inspired memory dynamics, and an explainable eight-signal retrieval system. The system runs offline with zero configuration and works with any OpenAI-compatible LLM or embedding model, whether cloud or local.

🔍 Overview

SME organizes all memories into a continuous embedding space where writes automatically form density-driven Memory Regions that dynamically grow, split, and merge. Regions connect via graph links. Memories also maintain six semantic edge types forming a Memory Graph: reference, causal, dialogue, summary, parent-child, and neighbor. Memory dynamics layer Ebbinghaus reinforcement, time decay (without deletion), automatic merging, and long-term compression on top.

🧩 How It Works

Two-stage hybrid retrieval combines region-led recall with vector/BM25 (Chinese bigram)/metadata hybrid search, optional graph enhancement, and an eight-signal explainable ranking. The 1.3 retrieval update adds min-max hybrid fusion (measured at +2.5 to +4.2 percentage points accuracy across three seed A/B tests, with bias halved) and Personalized PageRank graph expansion following the HippoRAG 2 approach to surface bridging associations. Optional idle-time automatic reorganization (sleep-time compute) and ONNX int8 embeddings are available via the [onnx] extra.

Memory lifecycle includes configurable reinforcement, decay, merging, and compression. Memories are never deleted due to decay and can be restored from archive.

⚙️ Key Details

Extension Modules (12 total, all disabled by default for base behavior)

Module Function
Fact extraction Extracts structured facts from input
QA pair replay Replays question-answer pairs
Temporal knowledge graph Builds time-aware knowledge graphs
User profiling Maintains user profiles
Fact version correction Corrects fact versions over time
Noise suppression Filters noisy inputs
WAL incremental persistence Write-ahead log for durability
Storage backend Pluggable storage
REST + SDK API and Python SDK access
Observability Metrics and monitoring
Hierarchical context Multi-level context management
Multi-user isolation Isolates memory per user

Presets (7 configurations)

  • Chat assistant
  • Knowledge base dynamic
  • Knowledge base static
  • Embodied robot
  • All off
  • Static retrieval · UNITED
  • Real model · semantic priority

Interfaces

  • Python SDK
  • REST API (FastAPI) with official client
  • MCP (agent-native, one-line mount)
  • Web configuration center (python -m sme.api then open browser)

Chinese-Friendly Features

  • Chinese 1-2 gram BM25 keyword channel enabled by default
  • Document clause import for legal/medical knowledge base scenarios

Explainable Retrieval

Every hit includes a breakdown of eight signals: semantic, importance, freshness, weight, decay, hit_count, recency, and region.

🚀 Availability

Installation: Zero-config offline operation. After installing core dependencies, a built-in hashing embedding runs the basic pipeline with no model downloads or API keys.

Core dependencies: numpy, httpx, fastapi, uvicorn, networkx, python-multipart, hnswlib (in [ann] extra). Install via pip install -r requirements.txt or pip install -e . (with pip install -e ".[ann]" for ANN acceleration; region scaling automatically enables ANN, falling back to exact scan otherwise).

Requirements: Python ≥ 3.10, Windows or Linux.

💡 Why It Matters

  • Benchmarked head-to-head against Mem0 and bare RAG
  • All 101 configuration items and 7 presets are fully toggleable
  • Performance figures: WAL group commit 2,557 writes/sec (1.79×), ONNX int8 batch embedding 7.4×, memory graph hot path O(E)→O(deg) measured 127–159×, hashing retrieval p50 ~4 ms at 2k items
  • Runs entirely offline with zero external dependencies for the base path

#AIMemory #RAG #LLM #Embeddings #OpenSource

Source: jack66g/spatial-memory-engine

item.title: Five new developments in long-term AI memory and agent evolution
item.description:
Five new developments in long-term AI memory and agent evolution

Recent technical updates in artificial intelligence focus on improving how agents manage long-term memory, evolve their internal states, and handle stale data or corrupted inputs. These developments span architectural innovations for memory storage, learnable policies for memory transformation, governance strategies for conflicting facts, and the impact of data corruption on recall accuracy.

🔍 Overview of Memory Innovations

  • KV-LTM: A new memory tier stores raw session text plus the KV cache under a fixed reader model, answering queries by restoring cached sessions.
  • EvoDisco: Formulates agent memory evolution as evolutionary strategy discovery, allowing agents to learn which operators to apply rather than following a static schedule.
  • RegimeCouncil: An online router that arbitrates between local and global memory sharing scopes to manage stale facts without retraining the LLM.
  • Corrupted Memory Testing: A study testing whether intentionally corrupting training data prevents LLM agents from overfitting to recent events.

🧩 How It Works

KV-LTM Architecture This approach is complementary to retrieval and indexing. It treats text as the memory of record while using the cache as a recompute-free prefill accelerator. The design includes:

  • Storage records and budget-derived retention.
  • An append-only read path and bounded aggregation.
  • Analytical sizing where per-token state spans approximately 31K-328K bytes for pinned BF16 full-attention and latent-cached MLA configurations.
  • A per-user-year storage estimate of approximately 0.34-3.6 TB at a 30K-token/day scenario, compared to approximately 49 MB of raw text.

EvoDisco Policy A learnable policy conditions on current memory state and recent task history to select and instantiate one of four semantic operators:

Operator Function
Abstract Compress related memories
Refine Decompose overloaded entries
Bridge Connect weakly linked experiences
Reframe Reorganize retrieved reasoning chains

The policy updates via a bi-level fitness: an inner signal scores transformation quality, while an outer signal scores strategic efficacy over past decisions.

RegimeCouncil Governance This system addresses the “memory conflict governance” problem where stored facts go stale. It uses a paired-evidence router with three modules:

  • Local Advisor: Tracks the latest outcome on a queried fact alone.
  • Global Advisor: Pools recent outcomes across all stored facts.
  • Meta Governor: Defaults to the Local Advisor to avoid cross-fact interference but switches to the Global Advisor when global pooling shows a positive utility margin.

⚙️ Key Details and Results

  • KV-LTM Evaluation: Requires no persistent-cache implementation for logical QA evaluation. It uses per-session prefill to emulate valid cache reuse. System-level comparisons on LongMemEval indicate that commercial assistants often score below models reading history offline, consistent with content loss between write and read phases.
  • EvoDisco Performance: In a one-pass online plus frozen-transfer protocol on ALFWorld, WebShop, and LifelongAgentBench, EvoDisco outperforms strong memory baselines like MemP and MemRL. The largest gains are observed on ALFWorld, with improvements of +8.8 to +12.9 points over MemP and +16.4 to +17.9 points over MemRL.
  • RegimeCouncil Performance: Across LongMemEval update streams and historical drift tests on TempLAMA and TAQA, RegimeCouncil outperforms the better fixed-scope policy by 5.2-7.3 points on primary disagreement episodes. Ablations show that removing any of its three modules reduces accuracy by 2-7 points.
  • Dream Hypothesis Test: An agent using Claude Opus 5.5 stored learned information in text memory and rewrote it nightly from transcripts with 5-40% corruption. The results showed that corruption did not help the agent apply earlier learned tasks. Replacing details in 40% of turns lowered recall from 76% to 60%. Random-text corruption had no consistent effect because the model recognized it as corrupted and excluded it from memory.

💡 Why It Matters

These updates address critical inefficiencies in long-term AI interactions. KV-LTM trades storage for avoided re-prefill compute and write-time fidelity, solving the problem where personal assistants accumulate months of conversations but struggle with derivation and selection. EvoDisco moves beyond fixed memory operators, allowing agents to dynamically decide how to transform their memory based on strategic efficacy. RegimeCouncil provides a lightweight method to handle delayed feedback from stale facts without the complexity of full LLM retraining. Finally, the corruption testing suggests that pretrained models can easily separate corrupted text from real events, implying that fair tests of memory evolution require learners that cannot make this distinction as easily, such as those fine-tuned on specific corrupted data or operating in invented worlds.

#AIMemory #LLMAgents #KVCache #AIResearch #LongTermMemory

Source: KV-LTM: Persistent Per-Session KV Caches as Long-Term Memory for Personal Assistants Source: EvoDisco: Strategy Discovery for Evolving Agent Memory Source: RegimeCouncil: Paired-Evidence Routing For Memory Conflict Governance In LLM Agents Source: Can an LLM dream? Testing the overfitted brain hypothesis on an agent with text memory

item.title: Memgraph powers real-time GraphRAG with in-memory C++ graph engine and hybrid vector search
item.description:
Memgraph powers real-time GraphRAG with in-memory C++ graph engine and hybrid vector search

Memgraph is a high-performance, in-memory graph database that powers real-time AI context and graph analytics. Built in C/C++, it serves as the graph engine for GraphRAG pipelines, AI memory systems, and agentic workflows. It delivers sub-millisecond multi-hop traversals for any system that needs structured, connected context alongside semantic vector or text search. Memgraph provides both in a single query layer: built-in text and vector indexes for similarity search combined with full graph traversal.

🧩 How it works

The same architecture drives real-time graph analytics for fraud detection, network analysis, infrastructure monitoring, and other operational workloads where performance matters. Memgraph is fully compatible with Neo4j’s Cypher query language, ACID-compliant, and highly available. Built-in vector indexes power hybrid graph retrieval with similarity search in a single query, alongside text and geospatial indexes for keyword and location-aware queries.

⚙️ Key details

The MAGE algorithm library includes 40+ graph algorithms in C++, Python, and CUDA including PageRank, community detection, GNN-based link prediction, temporal graph networks, embeddings, and native ML. Atomic GraphRAG enables pivot search, graph expansion, ranking, and prompt assembly expressed as a single Cypher query. The LLM utility module provides graph-aware context formatting for large language models. The AI Toolkit includes integrations with popular agentic frameworks, MCP server, and ready-made components for building GraphRAG, AI memory, and agent workflows on top of Memgraph.

Real-time schema introspection: SHOW SCHEMA INFO returns the full graph ontology for Text2Cypher and AI agent integration. In-memory C/C++ engine provides sub-millisecond traversals with benchmarked performance. Deep-path traversals support accumulators and path filtering without additional application logic. Custom query modules can be extended with Python, Rust, and C/C++ code natively. Parallel query execution enables concurrent query processing for high-throughput workloads.

🚀 Availability

Native Parquet & JSONL loading allows data to be loaded directly from Parquet and JSONL files on local disk, S3, or HTTP endpoints. Streaming support ingests from Kafka, Pulsar, and RedPanda with dynamic graph algorithms that react to changes in real time. High availability is achieved through Raft-based coordination with automatic failover. Multi-tenancy provides isolated databases with per-tenant role assignments. Fine-grained access control offers role-based and label-based permissions at the node and edge level. Authentication & authorization supports SSO integration, user impersonation, and 30+ granular permissions. Memgraph is licensed under the Apache License 2.0 (APL), Business Source License 1.1.1 (BSL), and MIT Electric License (MEL). Memgraph GitHub repository is available at github.com/memgraph/memgraph. Documentation is hosted at memgraph.com/docs/. Discord community is available at memgr.ph/join-discord. Daily builds can be accessed at memgraph.github.io/daily-builds/. Docker is required to run Memgraph with one command. Memgraph starts with Memgraph Lab when installed via Docker.

#GraphRAG #GraphDatabase #AIMemory #Cypher #VectorSearch #GraphAnalytics

item.title: Guide to Building Production AI Memory Systems
item.description:
Guide to Building Production AI Memory Systems

AI language models are stateless, so every request starts from a blank slate. What feels like memory in a chat window is actually an application trick that resends earlier messages. To give assistants persistent, user‑specific knowledge, developers add a separate engineering layer called an AI memory system. This guide explains the components, workflow, and practical considerations for deploying such a system in production.

🔍 Overview

  • Definition – An AI memory system is a storage and retrieval layer that lets an AI application save useful information, retrieve the relevant parts later, and use them to improve future responses.
  • Stateless models – Large language models are stateless by design; every request receives a prompt, produces a completion, and retains nothing. This is true of GPT‑style models, Claude, Gemini, and open‑source models such as Llama and Mistral alike.
  • Illusion of chat memory – What looks like memory in a chat window is an illusion produced by the application, which resends the earlier messages with each new request. That approach hits a hard ceiling because context windows are finite, long prompts cost more and respond slower, and models tend to use information in the middle of a very long context less reliably than information at the edges.

🧩 How it works

The core of every memory system follows a six‑step pipeline:

Step Description
Capture After each interaction, an extractor decides whether anything is worth keeping and rewrites it as a clean, self‑contained statement (e.g., “Prefers deployment on AWS.”).
Store The statement and its metadata (user ID, timestamp, source, confidence) are stored in a vector database.
Index An embedding model converts the text into a vector, placing similar meanings close together.
Retrieve At query time the system looks for the closest matches, then re‑ranks them by relevance, recency, and importance.
Inject The top memories are formatted into the prompt within a strict token budget.
Generate The language model generates a response using the injected memories; the memory lives in the prompt for minutes and is limited by the context window.

⚙️ Key details

  • External decision making – The memory system decides what to save, where to keep it, and what to place in front of the model on each turn.
  • Memory types –
    • Episodic memory lets an agent learn from experience rather than start over each time.
    • Distilled facts and domain knowledge such as “the user writes Python” or “refunds are allowed within 30 days.”
  • Memory updates – New facts are compared with old ones; duplicates are merged, contradictions are resolved, and stale items are expired.
  • Production definition – A governed data service with write policies, retrieval quality metrics, expiration rules, access controls, and user‑facing edit and delete tools.

💡 Why it matters

  • Without a memory system, developers must rely on ever‑growing prompts, which incur higher costs, slower responses, and reduced reliability of information deep inside the context.
  • An external memory can persist for months or years, enabling assistants to adapt to individual users over long periods.
  • Adding a memory layer transforms a stateless language model into an assistant that remembers preferences, policies, and domain facts across sessions.

#AImemory #LLM #ProductionAI

Source: AI Memory Systems: The Practical Guide to Architecture and Real-World Examples - Dealon.ai

item.title: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Adds Memory Lifecycle Policies for Long‑Running Agents
item.description:
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Adds Memory Lifecycle Policies for Long‑Running Agents

Memory lifecycle policies help long‑running agents on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore stay effective by systematically managing what they remember and forget.

🔍 Overview

  • Agents generate memories from every conversation they conduct.
  • Without active management, agents accumulate outdated context, which can degrade response quality and create compliance risks.
  • Real‑world examples: a customer‑support agent referenced a billing dispute resolved four months earlier, and another agent repeated superseded deployment advice from an old runbook.

🧩 How it Works

  • Memory storage: AgentCore stores information using two primary strategies – Summary and Episodic – each as individual entries tied to specific agent‑user sessions.
  • Additional categories: Semantic and Procedural memories are also part of the model, with distinct retention needs.
  • Scoring formula: A decay‑based score (0.0–1.0) balances three intuitions: recent memories matter, recently used memories matter more, and frequently retrieved memories add signal. Scores drop sharply in the first weeks then level off; an old memory accessed often can still score well.

⚙️ Policy Mechanics

  • TTL expiration runs first, automatically deleting records older than a configured time‑to‑live value.
  • AgentCore does not provide built‑in auto‑delete TTL, but it exposes system timestamp fields (x‑amz‑agentcore‑memory‑createdAt) that support BEFORE filters for pruning.
  • A pruner queries records with a BEFORE filter, then deletes those beyond the TTL.
  • After TTL pruning, the scoring step flags records below a configurable threshold for consolidation or further pruning.
  • Default configuration: pruneDays = 45, threshold = 0.3 → decay_rate ≈ 0.02676.

📊 Memory Types & Default Retention

Memory Type Typical TTL (default) Remarks
Episodic 90 days Stores raw session events
Summary 30–60 days Consolidated view of episodic data
Semantic 6–12 months Higher‑level concepts
Procedural No TTL (retain indefinitely) Reflections tied to episodic memory; lowest volume, highest value

🚀 Deployment Guide

  • A deployable architecture combines AgentCore memory, AWS Step Functions, and Amazon Bedrock to run a nightly lifecycle workflow.
  • By the end of the walkthrough you will have an AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) stack and a framework for managing agent memory as a managed resource.
  • The complete code is available in the GitHub repository.
  • Targeted agents: high‑volume interaction bots such as customer‑support agents, sales advisors, and IT help‑desk bots.
  • For lower‑volume agents (e.g., personal assistants) you might start with simple TTL expiration and GDPR compliance alone.
  • All thresholds and TTLs are configurable to match the agent’s needs.

💡 Why It Matters

  • Prevents outdated context from contaminating responses, protecting both quality and compliance.
  • Reduces unnecessary compute by pruning memories before scoring.
  • Provides a systematic, configurable approach to retain high‑value procedural knowledge while discarding stale information.
  • Enables long‑running agents to remain effective over weeks or months without manual intervention.

#AmazonBedrock #AgentCore #AImemory #AWS #LLMops

Source: Designing lifecycle policies for AgentCore memory | Amazon Web Services
